q: how does a jet engine work
how does a jet engine actually work
how do jet engines produce thrust
how does a turbine engine work
what are the stages of a jet engine
how does a turbofan engine work
how do jet engines generate thrust explained simply
what is the principle behind jet engines
a: A jet engine operates on the principle of Newton's Third Law — for every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction. It works by taking in air, compressing it, mixing it with fuel, burning the mixture, and expelling the hot exhaust gases at high speed out the back, which pushes the engine (and the aircraft) forward. The process occurs in four main stages: intake, compression, combustion, and exhaust. First, air enters through the fan at the front. In a turbofan engine (the most common type on commercial aircraft), a large fan acts like a ducted propeller, accelerating a portion of air around the core (bypass air) to generate a significant amount of thrust directly. The remaining air enters the core of the engine. Next, in the compression stage, a series of rotating compressor blades (rotors) and stationary blades (stators) progressively squeeze the air, increasing its pressure by up to 40 times. This compressed air then enters the combustion chamber, where fuel (typically kerosene-based Jet-A) is injected and ignited. The burning mixture expands rapidly. In the exhaust stage, the hot, high-energy gases pass through a turbine section. The turbine extracts some of that energy to spin the compressor and fan at the front via a central shaft — this is what makes the engine self-sustaining. After passing through the turbine, the remaining hot gases accelerate through a nozzle at the rear, producing thrust. Modern high-bypass turbofan engines generate most of their thrust from the bypass air (the air that goes around the core), making them quieter and more fuel-efficient than older turbojet designs. The entire process is a continuous cycle, and once started, a jet engine sustains itself as long as fuel and air are supplied.
